division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.note: Consulting detective living at 221B Baker Street; narrator Watson's friend; reads the hat and the stone.

characters.name: Dr. Watson
characters.note: First-person narrator and Holmes's companion, a doctor who visits Baker Street and joins the investigation.

characters.name: Peterson
characters.note: Honest commissionaire who finds the hat and goose on Tottenham Court Road and brings them to Holmes; his wife finds the stone.

characters.name: Henry Baker
characters.note: Middle-aged, grizzled, well-to-do-once gentleman who lost the hat and goose; member of the Alpha Inn goose club; visits Baker Street in a Scotch bonnet.

characters.name: John Horner
characters.note: 26-year-old plumber wrongly accused of stealing the blue carbuncle from the Countess of Morcar's jewel-case; the Horner of the Assizes case.

characters.name: Countess of Morcar
characters.note: Owner of the blue carbuncle, lost at the Hotel Cosmopolitan; offers a £1000 reward.

characters.name: James Ryder
characters.note: Upper-attendant (head attendant) at the Hotel Cosmopolitan who stole the stone and hid it in a goose; gives the false name John Robinson when approached at Covent Garden; not the Ryder of the court report giving evidence (that reading is in the newspaper).

characters.name: Catherine Cusack
characters.note: Maid to the Countess of Morcar; gave evidence at the trial and told Ryder of the stone; Ryder's accomplice.

characters.name: Inspector Bradstreet
characters.note: Police inspector of B division who arrested Horner; mentioned in the newspaper report only.

characters.name: Breckinridge
characters.note: Covent Garden poultry salesman with side-whiskers who bought the geese from Mrs. Oakshott and sold them on; not the goose's buyer for the Alpha.

characters.name: Windigate
characters.note: Ruddy, white-aproned landlord of the Alpha Inn, host of the goose club; bought geese from Breckinridge.

characters.name: Mrs. Oakshott
characters.note: Poultry supplier at 117 Brixton Road, married to Oakshott; James Ryder's sister, who sold the geese.

characters.name: Mrs. Hudson
characters.note: Holmes's landlady at Baker Street; only mentioned.

characters.name: Maudsley
characters.note: Ryder's former associate who had served time in Pentonville and lived in Kilburn; only mentioned.

characters.name: the goose
aliases: the white goose with a barred tail
characters.note: White goose with a black bar across the tail that swallowed the stone; it is an animal that is present in the action and carries the plot.

locations.name: 221B Baker Street
locations.note: Holmes and Watson's sitting-room, where the hat is examined and the final confrontation takes place.

locations.name: Tottenham Court Road
locations.note: Street where Peterson saw the stranger lose his hat and goose at about four o'clock on Christmas morning.

locations.name: the Alpha Inn
locations.note: Small public house near the Museum in Bloomsbury; home of Henry Baker's goose club.

locations.name: Covent Garden Market
locations.note: Market where Breckinridge's stall stands and where the confrontation with Breckinridge and Ryder occurs.

locations.name: Hotel Cosmopolitan
locations.note: Hotel where the Countess's jewel-case was rifled; only mentioned as the scene of the theft.

locations.name: Brixton Road
locations.note: Mrs. Oakshott's house and poultry yard, where Ryder hid the stone in the goose.

brief.tone: Wintry Christmas-season mystery: cold streets, warm firelit rooms, dry humour and a moral undertone of mercy.
depiction_rules: Holmes and Watson are shown in Victorian dress; Holmes in his purple dressing-gown or ulster at home and out of doors.
The blue carbuncle is a small, intensely brilliant blue stone, shown as a point of light, not a large gem.
The goose is a plain white bird with a black bar across the tail; no gore in the scenes with the goose.
Ryder's confession and near-collapse may show distress but no violence beyond his fall into the rug.
Holmes's deductions from the hat are shown as scrutiny with a lens, not as spectacle.

era.name: London, late Victorian, the days after Christmas
era.people: Londoners of all classes: a commissionaire, a plumber, a salesman, a publican, a hotel attendant, and gentlemen in frock-coats and Scotch bonnets.
era.dress: Heavy wool ulsters, cravats, top hats, bowler and billycock hats, frock-coats, aprons for tradesmen, long skirts for women.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit streets and shops, fanlights over doors, public houses with private bars, Covent Garden stalls under hanging lamps, a four-wheeler cab, clay pipes, basket-chairs, a strong-box.
era.technology: Gas lighting and coal fires; newspapers and advertisements in evening papers; no electric lighting except as a simile; no telephone; hansom and four-wheeled cabs.
